name: Jade Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Kestrel Auto, a busy independent garage in the suburbs with four bays and a waiting list most weeks. Dev, the owner, has me on services, suspension, timing belts with supervision, and anything where the fault code needs looking up, because I'm quick on the tablet. I use an AI app every day to turn fault codes and forum posts into a short list of likely causes, and then the older guys tell me which one it actually is. My hands are still catching up with my head, but I love the moment a car that came in on a tow truck drives out.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Sam, who works in a call centre for an energy company, answering billing calls. We've got around four months saved and rent a two-bed so I can keep tools in the spare room. At weekends I've started doing small mobile jobs, batteries and brake pads on driveways, for neighbours. It's maybe a hundred and fifty extra a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool, not a revolution, and people should stop panicking or celebrating. At work I'd keep using the app and showing Dev what it saves. Online I'd post a few before-and-after jobs from my weekend work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine, but Sam's call centre has already brought in an automated chat for simple billing questions. Even a small change takes the easy calls away and leaves the angry ones. AI doesn't have to change the world to make my partner's call centre job worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Kestrel, keep the weekend jobs growing a bit, and keep saving about a hundred and fifty a month. I'd ask Dev for the timing chain course so I can do bigger jobs on my own. Sam and I would keep an eye on their team numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for Sam, fine for me. It's a mixed feeling, like a good day at work with a bad phone call at lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's happening in Sam's team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two people left in the summer and weren't replaced, because the chat handles the simple stuff. Sam says the calls left are harder and the targets haven't changed. It's wearing them down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you grow the weekend jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly. I've got insurance for it now and a decent jack. I'd like it to cover a holiday a year.

I'd post **before-and-after** photos of my weekend driveway jobs.
think: Even small automation makes Sam's **call centre** job harder.
My own work at Kestrel feels **fine** for now.
do: Grow **weekend mobile jobs** and save about a hundred and fifty monthly.
Ask Dev for the **timing chain** course to take on bigger jobs.
feel: Feels **uneasy for Sam** but fine for herself.
S0.quote: AI doesn't have to change the world to make my partner's call centre job worse.
fieldNote: Her worry centres on **Sam's job**, already touched by automated chat.
She's building **weekend income** steadily and carefully.
She uses AI daily but trusts **older mechanics** for the final call.

steps.text: Grow weekend mobile jobs to cover a holiday a year
Ask Dev for the timing chain course
Save about a hundred and fifty a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real change and everyone should learn the tools, it's not a choice. At work I'd help Dev set up AI quoting and parts ordering. Online I'd share tips for other mechanics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm okay, maybe better off, because I'm already the one using it. Sam's the worry, since answering customers is right there on the list. My job gets easier with AI, and my partner's job is the one AI was built to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up Dev's quoting system in the first few months, ask for a pay bump, and grow my mobile jobs into a proper side business. I'd help Sam look at other work, maybe the energy firm's field team or a course. Savings up to five months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because of Sam. Excited about work, scared at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sam that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'll be all right, and that I'll cover rent for a while if needed. Sam would hate that, they're proud. We'd make a list of jobs to look at together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your side business grew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then maybe Sam could do the bookings and the accounts for it. That's thinking work AI does too, though. Ha, it always comes back round.

I'd share **tips** online for other mechanics and help Dev set things up.

**Sam's job** answering customers is exactly what AI is built for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow this down and help people, quickly. I'd post practical stuff, not panic. At work I'd tell Dev we need a plan for the robots in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, Sam's job is gone by 2028, I'm pretty sure. Mine changes but holds until the robots in 2031. My partner loses work first, and three years later the robots come for my bay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the mobile business hard while people still want a human on their driveway, and save everything. Sam would retrain fast, maybe into something hands-on like electrical or care. I'd look at how to service the robots, because someone has to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be doing a lot, but it's a lot to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays, then the second-bed flat. We'd move somewhere smaller and I'd store tools in a lock-up. Rent's the big one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you support both of you on your wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while, with the side jobs. Not forever, and not once the robots come.

say: I'd call for **slowing down** and helping people quickly.
I'd tell Dev we need **a plan** for robots in 2031.
think: **Sam's job** answering billing calls is likely gone by 2028.
My bay work holds until **robots** arrive three years later, in 2031.
do: Push the **mobile business** hard and save everything.
Help Sam **retrain** into electrical or care work.

S2.quote: My partner loses work first, and three years later the robots come for my bay.
fieldNote: She expects a **household earner** to lose work within two years.
She'd lean on her **mobile business** during the gap.

steps.text: Push the weekend mobile repair business to full weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years, so let's use them to retrain and plan. I'd share guides online. At work I'd be the one pushing for new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years helps Sam most, they could train properly. For me, robots at 2034 mean eight years of bay work and building the side business. Five years is enough for my partner to retrain properly, and that changes everything for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help Sam start a course in the first year and keep saving. I'd build the mobile business and look at robotics servicing courses later. Maybe we'd delay having kids a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in control. I'd have lists everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why delay kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because we'd want at least one steady income first. Five years is enough to get there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do at work first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get Dev to buy the new diagnostic kit early, so we're the garage that knows it. That buys a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a good runway, so let's make it count. I'd talk to mechanics online about what skills to build. I'd keep pushing Dev to modernise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is enough for me to own a small mobile business and for Sam to change careers. Ten years is long enough to build my own small business before the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the mobile business over five years, keep working at Kestrel part-time, and save steadily. Sam would retrain over a couple of years. I'd learn about servicing robots when the time comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. It feels doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the business in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe it turns into managing robot repairs, or something else. I'd keep it flexible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still have kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably around thirty-two. Ten years gives time.

S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to build my own small business before the robots arrive.

steps.text: Grow the mobile repair business over five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Sam's job goes first and mine follows fast. What would help is quick, paid retraining and support while one of us is out of work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about couples. Everyone asks about my job, but in our house the real risk is my partner's call centre job.

She moves fast with **plans and lists**, building her side business in each scenario.
Her mood follows **Sam's job** more than her own.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Sam's job goes first and hers follows.
